rules.statement: When the form of persisted bytes varies (e.g. PKCS#8 private vs. SubjectPublicKeyInfo public vs. X.509 DER), store an explicit encoding discriminator with the bytes and dispatch on it instead of guessing the format by trying one import and falling back to another on exception.
rules.why: Try-import-and-fall-back uses exceptions over cryptographic imports for control flow and leaves the stored form ambiguous; an explicit discriminator makes decoding deterministic.
rules.check: Look for deserializers that wrap ImportPkcs8PrivateKey/ImportSubjectPublicKeyInfo (or similar) in try/catch and retry another format, or persisted key records that have no field saying how their bytes decode.

rules.statement: Model independent properties (for example crypto family and public-vs-private storage container) as separate persisted discriminators rather than combining them into compound values of one enum or constant set (such as `rsa-public`).
rules.why: Combining orthogonal axes fragments the taxonomy, multiplies constants, and breaks mappings that are keyed on only one of the axes.
rules.check: Look for new type constants or enum members that encode two concepts at once (e.g. `<family>-public`, `<family>-pem`) when a separate field for the second concept would do.

rules.statement: An import path for caller-supplied asymmetric keys must accept public material only and reject any input carrying a private part: a JWK with `d`, a PEM private key, or a certificate that has a private key.
rules.why: Importing private key material is a separate threat model (reversible storage, escrow) that is out of scope; public-only by construction guarantees no private or symmetric material enters through import.
rules.check: In code that parses caller-supplied JWK/PEM/certificate key material for registration or import, verify there is an explicit rejection of private components (JWK `d`, `PRIVATE KEY` PEM labels, X509Certificate2.HasPrivateKey) and of symmetric (`oct`) keys.

rules.statement: Do not wrap a bare public key in a synthesized self-signed certificate to fit a certificate-only storage or validation path; store the bare key (e.g. as SPKI) directly.
rules.why: A synthesized certificate fabricates metadata (subject, validity) that the key owner never supplied.
rules.check: Look for CertificateRequest.CreateSelfSigned or similar used to wrap a JWK or public key received from a caller.

rules.statement: Represent an extensible set of format or kind names as open string constants that each implementation declares support for, not a closed enum, and check a requested name against the declared list at every entry point using ordinal comparison, rejecting unlisted names with an error that lists the accepted values.
rules.why: Packages can add new formats (PKCS #12, OpenSSH keys, key-vault references), so the vocabulary is open; checking at every entry point keeps behavior consistent, and ordinal comparison keeps names exact (`JWK` is not `jwk`).
rules.check: Look for closed enums used for extensible format names, entry points (validators, services) that skip checking the name against the implementation's declared list, case-insensitive or culture-sensitive comparisons of these names, or rejection messages that don't list the supported values.

rules.statement: Apply at-rest data protection to all stored key material, public material included, rather than skipping protection for keys considered non-secret.
rules.why: Protection is an at-rest concern applied uniformly to all material regardless of confidentiality, so storage and decoding work the same way for every key.
rules.check: Look for persistence code that writes public key or certificate bytes without the data protector used for private keys, or that branches on public/private to skip protection.
